query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying the eutectic high-entropy alloy with a ductile element (e.g., adding a small weight percentage of Cu) will induce targeted boundary segregation, forming ultra‐thin, ductile interfacial layers along the dual-phase lamellar colony boundaries. This modification is expected to enable enhanced dislocation transmission across internal interfaces, thereby reducing dislocation pile-ups, mitigating local stress concentrations, and in turn overcoming the limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness without sacrificing—and potentially even increasing—the strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure, where internal phase boundaries promote dislocation pile-ups that cause local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic failure during room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled microalloy addition (for example, 2–4 at% of Cu) during alloy processing designed to segregate preferentially to the lamellar interfaces, thereby modifying the local interfacial chemistry and structure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under standard mechanical loading conditions, representative of typical operating environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of ultra-thin, ductile interfacial layers at the boundaries between the dual phases within the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The segregated ductile element lowers the interfacial energy and weakens the barrier to dislocation transmission, allowing dislocations to glide more continuously across phase boundaries. This reduces the accumulation of dislocations (pile-ups) at the interfaces, alleviates local stress concentrations, and helps prevent microcrack nucleation and propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility (e.g., increased elongation to failure) while maintaining or slightly increasing the yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The original eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibits limited ductility and brittle behavior due to severe dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries that lead to microcracking under tensile load.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect depends on achieving a uniform, ultra-thin interfacial layer that does not form deleterious phases. If the microalloying element does not segregate effectively, or excess amounts lead to embrittling compounds, the mechanical improvements may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal type and concentration of the microalloying element for forming effective ductile interfacial layers remains to be precisely determined, as does the exact quantitative improvement in ductility relative to strength retention.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy: one set with the microalloy addition (e.g., 2–4 at% Cu) and one set as an unmodified control. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to verify that the added element indeed segregates to the internal lamellar boundaries forming an ultra-thin ductile layer. Subsequently, conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both sample sets, recording stress-strain curves, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure.
measurements: High-resolution TEM and EDS analysis of interfacial layers
Tensile stress-strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation to failure)
Quantitative analysis of dislocation distributions and pile-up density near boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microalloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility (for instance, less than a 20% increase in elongation to failure) relative to the control, or if mechanical testing reveals a decrease in strength or similar levels of dislocation pile-ups and microcracking compared to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
